item.title: Creating MTF's...: Re: Creating MTF's...
item.content:encoded:
Could I possibly create a MTF and create a dossier detailing what they do/would do

MTFs typically don't have their own dossier pages. Do you have an example of the kind of page you would make for a dossier?

Then write tales + mission reports on encounters my MTF has with SCP's as well as backstories on important figures within the MTF?

You should write tales/after action reports first, since a dossier would be just a laundry list information dump without the background stories existing. Keep in mind that your material needs to entertain the audience with a story, rather than a list of facts about a group they haven't committed their interest to yet.

item.title: My first SCP failed, can anyone give me advice about why?: Re: My first SCP failed, can anyone give me advice about why?
item.content:encoded:
it looked like it would take months

Like Zyn mentioned, strong ideas tend to attract more crit faster (so silence can itself be an indicator that an idea might need improving) but it's worth mentioning good writing frequently does take ages; it's a process more than an act. If you check the comments section, author's notes for many SCPs mention months or even years of off-and-on development.

You'll see the occasional bolt-of-inspiration idea thrown together over a weekend, but that's the exception, not the rule.

item.title: My first SCP failed, can anyone give me advice about why?: Re: My first SCP failed, can anyone give me advice about why?
item.content:encoded:
I tried doing the greenlight thing and it looked like it would take months.

Greenlights can be obtained extremely quickly if the concept is good enough. You can use the IRC chatrooms for real-time responses; plenty of authors seek fast greenlights that way.

I did try to contact them, but got very little back, so I got impatient.

Whom did you contact, and did you ever request staff assistance with being matched with a reviewer?

item.title: Ideas for execution of a "Monster What Kills You" skip: Ideas for execution of a "Monster What Kills You" skip
item.content:encoded:
At some point in the near future (perhaps after the posting of one or more other articles) I would really like to take on the writing challenge of making a "classic monster" skip interesting. It's such a commonly-avoided topic that I can't help but be enticed to try and make it work. Here are some qualities such a hypothetical monster would have to include, as part of the challenge:

  • Very little in the way of motivation, i.e. a predator or something similar
  • Irrepressibly violent tendencies towards humans, i.e. this is just a thing what kills you
  • No cop-outs or deceptions as to its nature, i.e. it is exactly what it seems to be.

Given these constraints, the most plausible avenue to success seems to be setting the monster within a narrative that stands on its own. However, even that feels like cheating to me, as by shifting the focus of the article from the monster to the story, I've effectively conceded that it is simply impossible to make a monster interesting nowadays.

Does anyone know of some modern skips that could provide inspiration? Do you have any ideas about what would be necessary to make this challenge possible? Do you believe it is possible at all? Should I abort this ill-conceived venture at once??? Please let me know.

If it goes well, I might try to do the same for an x-man.

item.title: My first SCP failed, can anyone give me advice about why?: Re: My first SCP failed, can anyone give me advice about why?
item.content:encoded:
I'll preface this by saying I'm not an official critter, nor a seasoned author (I've written one SCP that did… okay, but wasn't highly received.)

I think the clinical tone could use some work. Moreover, some of the dialogue feels a little bit clunky at times. Some parts are difficult to read because the article tends to repeat itself a lot. For example, twice you mention mention how the substance will corrode into unglazed ceramic. Additionally, oxytocin/serotonin/dopamine levels are repeatedly mentioned, when instead you could say something like:

Instances of SCP-5245-2 share a similar bodily composition to SCP-5245, complete with
identical hormones and neurotransmitters.

I also feel like there's designation bloat. SCP-5245-1 is a copy of the mask that's mentioned once, then never again. I'd lose that, and simply change SCP-5245-2 to SCP-5245-1. You could say:

When in the proximity of an individual that lacks a face covering, SCP-5245 will
manufacture an identical copy of the mask from its body and forcibly place it upon
the victim (hereby referred to as an instance of SCP-5245-1.)

Overall, I think there's a good idea, but the conclusion left me feeling very underwhelmed. I'd recommend visiting the Idea Critique Forum to see what the critters think (who are much better writers then I'll ever be). Keep corresponding with them until you get greenlights, then write a draft, then go to the Draft Critique Forum. Then, if you've gotten good feedback, post to the main site.

item.title: Looking for someone to rewrite The Kephart Arc: Looking for someone to rewrite The Kephart Arc
item.content:encoded:
Hi everyone!

So, back during JamCon One, I wrote one segment of the same story for each prompt, each an SCP focusing on a pair of researchers investigating a creepy company. They are sequential on the mainlist, SCP-3643, SCP-3644, and SCP-3645. I reread them recently and I think they're some of my worst work, because I was attempting to write in a way I normally don't, but they also don't deserve to be deleted. I won't delete them if anyone wants to take a crack at rewriting them and trying to fix some of their flaws. Does anyone want to try?

item.title: SCP Reference Help: Re: SCP Reference Help
item.content:encoded:
Thank you for the response! Right yeah, exactly. The events that occur are more important than the things that they occur upon. But if you'll pardon the metaphor: That's why I'm trying to find a heading to set sail. Because I wish to find uncharted waters, but I can't do that if I don't know what's ahead of me. That is to say, I don't wish to come anywhere near any similar SCP.

You mention that "my ideas are fine for that reason". I hope what that means is that this is somewhat true, my "jumping off" concept is original enough to weave it's own tale. But I will take that with a grain of salt. I will have to go through an arduous process to spin a story that's foundation worthy, but I don't want to tread any lines already made. Sincerely, I thank you again.

Edit: after looking it over a few times I realized the context of the response. So I edited the above a little to better reflect my concern with that understanding. So yes, I'm still curious of similar anomalies, but I comprehend the tale is more important than the characters.

item.title: SCP Reference Help: Re: SCP Reference Help
item.content:encoded:
I think you should be less concerned with the basic anomalous properties of your object and more with the story that it's couched in. It doesn't particularly matter if we have two magnifying glass SCPs if they tell different stories. Your ideas are fine for that reason.

I mean, I'm not particularly speaking to the cohesion of the ideas themselves — the invulnerable man trope doesn't particularly interest me and a magnifying glass that sees things really good seems pretty straightforward. Just a fair warning, although all this should be ironed out in the idea crit process.
